newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Rite Aid to buy two drugstore chains in South.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rite Aid to buy two drugstore chains in South.

text.p: Drugstore giant Rite Aid Corp., continuing its aggressive expansion, Monday announced plans to buy two privately held rival chains in the South for between $325 million and $340 million.

The deals to buy New Orleans-based K&B Inc. and Tuscaloosa, Ala.-based Harco Inc. will give Rite Aid 3,963 stores in 31 states, strengthening its position as one of the nation's largest drugstore chains.

"The addition of two pre-eminent Southern drugstore chains gives Rite Aid a strong regional nucleus of operations and establishes a solid platform from which to expand our business in this fast-growing area of the country," Chairman Martin Grass said in a news release.

The deals came as a surprise because Rite Aid previously had said it did not plan any acquisitions in 1997 following its late-1996 purchase of West Coast-based Thrifty PayLess Inc. for more than $1.3 billion.

But in an interview, Grass said the integration of Thrifty PayLess was proceeding ahead of schedule and enabled the company to pursue the latest two transactions. He said Thrifty PayLess' central office has been pared down so far to 35 employees from 780.
"We originally had scheduled all calendar year to get integrated. Here it is July and we're just about done," he said.
The latest deals were set into motion when Rite Aid was approached by investment bankers representing K&B, Grass said.
"Sometimes you have to take advantage of an opportunity when it presents itself," he said.
Rite Aid originally did not disclose the value of the transactions, but Grass agreed with a Wall Street Journal estimate that they were worth between $325 million and $340 million.
Rite Aid said K&B and Harco are the nation's 13th and 17th largest drugstore chains, respectively, in terms of sales.

Together, K&B and Harco own more than 330 stores in Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi, Texas, Tennessee and Florida. Rite Aid said K&B had fiscal 1996 sales of $580 million from 186 stores and Harco had fiscal 1996 sales of $258 million.
Rite Aid said it expected the deals to add to earnings by the second quarter of next year. Before that, the deal will be neutral to earnings, Grass said.
Following completion of these acquisitions, all K&B and Harco stores will be operated under the Rite Aid banner and all their store employees will be retained.
However, Rite Aid said it will close the Harco and K&B corporate offices and transfer all headquarters functions to Rite Aid headquarters in Camp Hill, Pa.
Analysts said Rite Aid will have no problem blending the two chains into its operations.
"It's a drop in the bucket for them and it's an opportunity they couldn't pass up," said Eric Bosshard of Midwest Research-Maxus Group.
Grass said the latest transactions do not necessarily represent an aggressive push into the South, but noted "we find any part of the country appealing where we can get strong market share."

However, those opportunities are becoming increasingly scarce due to widespread consolidation in the previously fragmented industry. In addition to Rite Aid's acquisition of Thrifty PayLess, other big deals over the past year include CVS Corp.'s $2.8 billion purchase of Revco D.S. Inc. and J.C. Penney's acquisition of Eckherd Corp for $2.5 billion.
And in May, investment bank Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette bought a majority stake in Manhattan chain Duane Reade Holding Corp. for about $350 million.
Grass admitted that opportunites now are growing scarce.

"I keep saying there's less and less (opportunity)... but there obviously are some opportunities although they're getting very scarce - especially the quality of what is left. They're not necessarily all that appealing - at least to us," he said.
Shares of Rite Aid rose 44 cents to $48.44 in consolidated New York Stock Exchange midafternoon trading.
